chief_complaint: chronic cough, night sweats, and weight loss
hpi_details: 45M presents with a 4-week history of a productive cough (sometimes with blood streaks), drenching night sweats, fatigue, and a 10-pound weight loss. He recently emigrated from Southeast Asia.
social_hx: Recent immigrant, living in a crowded apartment

investigation_events.title: Urgent chest radiograph
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent chest radiograph is now available; airborne isolation and public-health notification should not be delayed while microbiologic testing is pending.

results.value: Right upper-lobe cavitary opacity with surrounding patchy infiltrate
results.note: Sputum AFB smear, culture, and NAAT remain pending

core_concepts: Classic symptoms: chronic cough (>2-3 weeks), hemoptysis, weight loss, fever, night sweats.
common_misconceptions: Assuming a negative PPD or IGRA rules out active TB in a severely ill or immunocompromised patient.
dangerous_errors: Failing to place the patient in airborne isolation (negative pressure room) immediately upon suspicion.
management_principles: Airborne isolation, Chest X-ray, Sputum AFB smears and cultures, GeneXpert.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 45M with a chronic productive cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, and weight loss. Recent immigrant.
reference_soap.objective: Thin, cachectic appearing. Bronchial breath sounds and crackles in the right upper lobe.
reference_soap.plan: Immediate airborne isolation. STAT Chest X-ray. Order 3 sputum AFB smears/cultures and NAAT. Notify public health.

learning_objectives: Identify classic symptoms of active TB and implement prompt infection control.

teaching.one_liner: Chronic cough with hemoptysis, night sweats, and weight loss in a patient from an endemic area.

must_ask.say: How long have you had the cough, and have you coughed up any blood?
Have you had drenching night sweats that soak your clothes or sheets?
Have you lost weight without trying?
Have you traveled from or lived in an area where tuberculosis is common, or been around anyone with TB?
Have you ever coughed up a large amount of blood at once?

history.answer: I've had this persistent cough for about four weeks now, and I've been losing weight without trying.
The cough started about a month ago and has gradually become more frequent and heavier.
It didn't begin after a cold or flu, and I have never experienced a cough lasting this long before.
I bring up a spoonful or two of thick yellowish phlegm every day, but it does not smell foul.
Over the past week I've noticed streaks of bright red blood mixed in the mucus, but never mouthfuls or cups of blood.
I cough throughout the entire day and night, and lying down flat doesn't seem to make it worse.
No, I do not have uncontrollable coughing fits, whooping sounds when I inhale, or vomiting after coughing.
Dusty environments make me clear my throat, but cold air, physical exertion, and pets don't specifically trigger it.
I haven't heard any whistling or wheezing sounds, though I get tired and winded more easily lately.
I haven't checked with a thermometer, but I feel flushed and feverish almost every late afternoon.
Yes, almost every night for the past three weeks I wake up drenched in sweat and need to change my clothes and sheets.
I have lost about ten pounds over the past month because my appetite has completely dropped off.
My chest feels somewhat sore and achy on the right side when I cough hard, but there is no sharp stabbing pain when I breathe in.
No runny nose, nasal congestion, or sensation of fluid dripping down the back of my throat.
I don't have heartburn, sour regurgitation into my mouth, or a sensation of a lump in my throat.
No, I can sleep comfortably on one pillow, and my feet and legs have not become swollen.
I do not take any blood pressure medications, ACE inhibitors, or regular prescription drugs.
I have never been diagnosed with or treated for tuberculosis, but it was common where I grew up in Southeast Asia.
A couple of roommates in my apartment have had lingering coughs, though none have mentioned a specific medical diagnosis.
I work general maintenance and warehouse tasks, with no heavy exposure to silica dust, toxic chemicals, birds, or mold.
I have never had asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema, or known food allergies.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any chronic medical conditions.
I have never undergone any surgical procedures and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter cough syrups, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I used to smoke about half a pack a day for roughly ten years, but I completely quit five years ago.
I only drink an occasional beer once or twice a month, and I have never used illicit drugs.
I moved here from Southeast Asia about six months ago and currently live in a crowded two-bedroom apartment with four other adults.
Both of my parents are alive in their seventies with high blood pressure, and there is no family history of lung disease or cancer.
Because of the blood and weight loss, I'm terrified that this could be lung cancer, and I'm very anxious about whether I might pass an infection to my roommates and family.

exam.finding: Thin, cachectic-appearing male who looks fatigued but is in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 37.8°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Mild conjunctival pallor without scleral icterus.
Nasal mucosa pink without discharge; posterior pharynx clear without erythema, cobblestoning, or post-nasal drainage.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Symmetrical chest wall expansion; increased tactile fremitus over the right upper lung field without chest wall tenderness.
Dullness to percussion over the right upper lung zone; resonant across all other lung fields.
Bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right upper lobe; normal vesicular breath sounds without wheezes in all other fields.
Regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
No digital clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral pitting edema in the lower extremities.
